implementation_notes: The Ruby stdlib has no future, so the requestor builds the structure by hand: a Mutex-protected Hash mapping the correlation id to a Thread::Queue (or a Thread::ConditionVariable plus its mutex), with the caller blocking in queue.pop(timeout: seconds), which returns nil when the deadline expires, and the transport's reader thread removing the entry and pushing the reply. concurrent-ruby's Promise/Future is the usual gem-level upgrade when the same shape is wanted with fulfill/value!(timeout) semantics and thread pools; the process-global interpreter lock still lets other threads run while one blocks, so the waiting is cheap for I/O-bound calls. Because the code is hand-written, the entry-removal path and the timeout path must be kept in one place or the table leaks.
pitfalls: Thread::Queue#pop(timeout:) is recent: on older rubies the wait must be built from Thread::ConditionVariable#wait with a deadline (or Timeout.timeout), and the expiry signal differs - nil versus a raised exception - so wrap the transport's wait in one place.

An exception raised inside the reader thread is invisible to the waiting caller, so the queue must carry error results or a sentinel value, otherwise the call hangs until its deadline with no diagnostic.
A plain Hash is not safe for concurrent mutation: every insert, lookup and delete must go through the mutex or a reply can be lost or the entry corrupted under JRuby/TruffleRuby and Ractors.

The ensure block removes the entry on every path, but a reply that already removed it and then pushes leaves a value in a queue nobody reads - that is the expected late-reply drop, not a leak of the table.
